title: The Kariakoo Restaurant Said Salim Bakhresa Bought in 1975
dek: After many small ventures failed, a former street-food seller from Zanzibar bought a restaurant in Dar es Salaam and stayed with food for fifty years.

story.event: Buying the Azam restaurant in Kariakoo, Dar es Salaam, after years of failed small ventures
story.summary: Said Salim Bakhresa, who left school at 14 and sold street food in Zanzibar, bought the Azam restaurant on Livingstone Street in Kariakoo, Dar es Salaam, in 1975 after many small ventures had failed in a largely state-run economy. The business formed Said Salim Bakhresa & Co in 1983 and bought its first flour mill in 1992 to supply its own bakery, later taking over state mills through privatisation and growing into the Bakhresa Group.
paragraphs: On 30 January 2026, the UTV programme Fahari Yetu aired an exclusive interview with Said Salim Bakhresa, then 78 and chairman of the Bakhresa Group, the company behind Azam flour. He went back to the start. His family's circumstances, he said, forced him out of school at 14 to support himself. He began by selling urojo and mishkaki in Zanzibar. "It was a small food business, but I believed in it," he recalled, in The Citizen's translation.

What he knew then was mostly what had not worked. When he started out, he said, many sectors of the economy were run by the state, and the climate was not friendly to private traders. "There was no small business I didn't attempt," he said, and many of his efforts failed; almost everything "seemed to hit a wall". When he moved from Zanzibar to the mainland he kept one idea with him: a restaurant of his own. Things, he said, were not easy at all.

In 1975 he bought one: the Azam restaurant on Livingstone Street in Kariakoo, Dar es Salaam. Accounts from the group and from its Swiss milling supplier describe it as a small, family-run restaurant. He stayed with the trade he already knew, food, and he is plain about what it cost him. He worked around the clock, he said, with no leisure, going only between work and home, once for three months in a row without stepping away from his schedule.

The restaurant became a base. The group's own timeline dates its bakery company, Azam Bakeries, to the same year, and its flagship, Said Salim Bakhresa & Co, to 1983. In 1992, according to Bühler, the Swiss company that supplied it, the business bought its first flour mill, to make flour for its own cake bakery. Later the company took over state-owned wheat, rice and maize mills through Tanzania's privatisation programme and, it says, turned them around.

In 2025 the group marked fifty years, counting from that restaurant. The Citizen reported that Bakhresa now heads more than 17 companies in Tanzania and nine other African countries. He said he never imagined it would grow so large, and he credited government support as well as his own effort.

quote.text: to amuse oneself in order that one may exert oneself, as Anacharsis puts it, seems right; for amusement is a sort of relaxation, and we need relaxation because we cannot work continuously.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Bakhresa counts months without leisure as part of how the business was built. Aristotle, borrowing from Anacharsis, says rest is taken for the sake of the work, because nobody can work continuously. Both take work seriously; they disagree about whether going without rest is part of doing it well.

reflection: The part of this story that may feel closest is the early part: the attempts that hit a wall, and an economy that did not seem built for someone starting small. What carried Bakhresa was not one clever move but an idea he kept close to his own trade, and fifty years of adding to it.

He is honest that he gave up leisure to do it. You do not have to copy that part to keep the rest. Aristotle's point is practical: the person who does the work is a body that has to recover, and the work goes better when it does.
invitation: Choose one evening this week that will end at home with no work in it, and tell one person at home which evening it is, so that someone else helps you keep it.

sources.title: Bakhresa opens up on how he built business empire in Tanzania
sources.supports: Report of Bakhresa's exclusive interview on UTV's Fahari Yetu, aired 30 January 2026, aged 78: leaving school at 14 because of family circumstances; selling urojo and mishkaki ('It was a small food business, but I believed in it'); leaving Zanzibar for the mainland and keeping the idea of a restaurant though things were 'not easy at all'; many sectors state-run and unfriendly to private entrepreneurs; 'there was no small business I didn't attempt'; many failures, 'seemed to hit a wall'; working around the clock with no leisure, three consecutive months; more than 17 companies in Tanzania and nine other African countries; never imagined the current size; credit to government support.

cross_checks.claim: In 1975 Bakhresa bought (or was running) the Azam restaurant in Dar es Salaam, the start of the group
He left school at 14 and started out selling street food in Zanzibar
Said Salim Bakhresa & Co, the flagship company, was formed in 1983
The business moved from a restaurant into milling, later acquiring state wheat, rice and maize mills through privatisation

research_notes: Bakhresa gives very few interviews, so the story leans on one: his UTV Fahari Yetu interview of 30 January 2026 as reported (and translated, presumably from Swahili) by The Citizen; the quotations are The Citizen's English wording. Billionaires.Africa (1 February 2026) reports the same interview with the same details and was read as a check but is not cited. The restaurant: Daily News (June 2025, from the group's head of public relations at the golden-jubilee launch) says he 'purchased Azam restaurant' on Livingstone Street, Kariakoo, in 1975; the group's board page says he started as 'a restaurant owner (Azam restaurant)' in downtown Dar es Salaam in 1975; Bühler and Food Business Africa (which repeats Bühler's sentence) say a small family-run restaurant in the port of Dar es Salaam in the mid-1970s. The story uses 1975 and Daily News's 'bought'. How the purchase was paid for is not documented anywhere I found, so funding is 'unknown' rather than the slate's 'bootstrapped'. The group's timeline lists Azam Bakeries under 1975 but its text says the bakery was 'founded in the early 1970s'; the story says only that the timeline dates it to 1975. Milling: the slate's framing (restaurant, then flour) holds, but the date of the first mill is given only by Bühler (1992, to supply the group's own cake bakery), so it is attributed to Bühler; Food Business Africa dates the food and beverage operations to SSB's formation in 1983 and gives no date for the privatisation purchases, so the story gives none. Age: The Citizen says he was 78 in January 2026, while Wikipedia gives a birth year of 1949 (which would make him 76 or 77); the story uses The Citizen's figure as reported and gives no birth year. Wikipedia says he left school at 14 to sell 'potato mix' (urojo is often called Zanzibar mix) and is used only as a supplementary cross-check. Workforce figures disagree widely (Wikipedia: more than 2,000; the group's board page: more than 8,000 direct employees; Daily News, quoting the group in 2025: 10,000 in Tanzania and 10,000 elsewhere), so the story gives no headcount, and likewise no turnover (board page: over USD 800 million; Daily News: USD 1.0 billion).
